analyst.author: BuriedTreys
analyst.text:
West Virginia / Auburn (Vegas)

Really odd body clock game to have these teams playing the last tip of the night at 9pm local. Auburn is off their first loss of the year to a good Arizona team, but the major concern was a Tigers frontcourt that allowed the Wildcats to corral nearly 40% of their misses. It also didn’t help their cause that Tahaad Pettiford and Kevin Overton combined to shoot 6-27 in a home game that was tied with ten minutes to go. While West Virginia may not have the individual backcourt defenders of Arizona, the Mountaineers are off a year where they ranked 18th nationally defensively and got much bigger in the frontcourt this offseason

We haven’t learned much about West Virginia given they enter this matchup with the 352nd Strength of Schedule, but this was a really intriguing team in the offseason, and that was before they got Boise State transfer Javan Buchanan and returning starter Brennan Lorient in the 5-in-5 market. The ‘Neers have an electric scoring backcourt behind sparkplug frosh Miles Sadler and multi-year P5 starter Finley Bizjack who can really help Ross Hodge turn the corner offensively as a coach. They will likely be a 2-way turnover monster, and if Sylla & Seini hold up at the Center spot, then West Virginia could be really sneaky shot volume team. There is still plenty of projection with how those Centers play up in competition, but the makeup and balance of this team is underrated in my opinion.

West Virginia will again be elite at pushing teams away from the rim under Ross Hodge, but Auburn is an extremely jumpshot-happy offense whose main source of paint points is on putbacks and second chances. The Mountaineers will also be strong at denying transition opportunities, and Auburn has shot quite poorly when forced to play in the halfcourt this season. The reality with Auburn’s offense is that it is likely going to live and die by the jumpshooting of their backcourt. When they’re hot, the Tigers will be able to hang in with pure shotmaking and offensive rebounds. When they are off, and it leaks over to the defensive side, Auburn is going to look very underwhelming at times.

I think my other worry with Auburn is if they are in for another year of really mediocre defense. Kevin Overton is fine as a defender, Ngoy will put up outrageous rates but cannot stay on the floor, but outside of those two, the level of individual defense with these players worries me (although I’ll leave the light on for frosh Caleb Williams on that side). They currently sit 36th defensively on KenPom but 50th on BartTorvik w/o preseason priors, and that’s with probably being fortunate from the arc on that side of the ball at a 28% 3PD%. Last year, opponents shot 36.7% from the arc and Auburn returns the same two guys in the backcourt, so are they really going to be that much better defending the perimeter?

West Virginia will also have a massive advantage, especially athletically, at the wing. Thomas Dowd has maintained his strong rebounding numbers that he posted at Troy, has been efficient from the perimeter, but there is still a massive athleticism delta between he and Adam Olsen compared to Brennan Lorient and company. Where Auburn will have to win this is on the glass which is maybe the biggest question mark of this West Virginia team. Mo Sylla has looked good now that he is healthy, but it’s tough not to look good when you have his pedigree and you have played Niagara, Stetson, and Mercer. The big bodies underneath for Auburn are a much more physically imposing battle, and if the Tigers are going to pull this out, it likely comes from a combination of their backcourt shotmaking and a rebounding advantage

The main external factors are how Auburn bounces back off a loss (6-10 ATS off loss last year) compared to how West Virginia plays against their first P5 opponent. Even with blowing out Niagara and Stetson, West Virginia has still only risen two spots in KenPom since the start of the year. They have probably been fortunate defensively from both the 3P line (27.8% 3PD%) and FT line (50% FT ‘defense’), but when you are coached by Ross Hodge it is hard not to see you being very good on that side of the ball.

While Sadler is putting a ridiculous 57.8% Asst% (2nd nationally to Fears), he did enter college with some potential turnover concerns. There may be matchups later on in the year like the ice defenses of Houston, Iowa State, and TCU where he is likely to struggle, but Auburn is going to be a pretty passive defense at the point of attack. I was pretty surprised to see the line come back towards the Tigers, so I may have to get involved on the West Virginia side as a slight dog. I know the defense of that team will travel, they’ll drag Auburn into a rockfight halfcourt game, and they could be the better offense in that type of environment. As long as they don’t get clubbed on the interior or suffer an incendiary Auburn 3P performance, WVU should look like the better team overall in my opinion.

analyst.author: BuriedTreys
analyst.text:
Michigan State @ Tennessee

Really interesting matchup given these two teams could not be viewed more differently by the CBB public. Sparty just notched arguably the biggest win of the season for any team while the Vols experienced an extremely troubling scrimmage season and have only played the 355th SOS to-date. The fact that this is at Thompson Boling Arena is probably what makes this most susceptible to a potentially screwy outcome.

After Tennessee blew out Wofford and Radford to start the year, there was some optimism around them potentially finding some of the form available to a team with as much talent as they have. They then allowed a Tennessee State team who managed only 0.76 PPP against Murray State to post over 1 PPP at home. The glass half full folks may call that a flat/lookahead spot. The glass half empty ones may say that Tennessee State shot 26% from the arc on THIRTY 3PAs and only lost by two possessions. The most troubling part of that Tennessee State game was the fact that the Vols turned it over on more than 22% of possessions and allowed a 45% OREB%. If you cannot hold onto the ball, and you are not going to get on the glass, then boy is Michigan State’s physicality going to be a very unfun game for you. The question with this team all year will be how do these players mesh offensively, and can Rick Barnes teach a collection of offensive-minded players how to defend?

Defensively, you’ll see a fair bit of similarities between these schemes. Both units are going to be elite at keeping opponents out of the key (both rank T25 in Haslam Defensive Near Proximity Frequency), both are going to be physical and foul-happy at times, these coaches tend to be strong in transition denial, and both have questions around their rim protection at the Center spot. Tennessee has been playing much faster offensively—more than 3 seconds faster Average Offensive Possession Length than last year. How much of that is due to playing midmajors, or is it Barnes realizing that they probably do not want to get overly bogged down in the halfcourt? If the Vols cannot create live ball turnovers and/or runout opportunities, then it is probably advantage to a Sparty team who has the best point guard in the country with Jeremy Fears.

One interesting aspect of this matchup is that the primary weakness of both these teams is at the Center spot. The Vols desperately needed Jalen Washington in the 5-in-5 market, and regardless of how well Sparty defended at the rim against Duke, it was a whole lot more Jordan Scott and the wings than Bonke and Taylor. Fully healthy, Sparty also has the much better defensive wing group to support some of that questionable rim protection—Scott just had one of the best individual defensive performances of any player in the country all season…against Duke. DeWayne Brown would have been an awesome Power Forward complement to Washington underneath, but he is somewhat forced to eat a lot of minutes at the 5 because the other options all have questions about translating at the P5 level. Jordan Scott is also questionable for this one with a bad shoulder and his status looms large especially on the defensive end for Sparty.

Early on in the year, I am very conscientious of teams who have not really seen much adversity in terms of making comebacks or winning through poor efficiency games. To be clear, I am not taking anything away from Sparty’s impressive performance against Duke. There is also a bit of a snowball effect when you come out hitting shots early, your opponent is ice cold, you have emphatic blocks at the rim and get your fans going like Fears and company did. On the road, what happens if the roles are reversed and it’s Tennessee who comes out hot? For all the worries that people have with this team, shotmaking may be at the very bottom of the list. Hill, Harris, Lundblade, and Ames all have had their share of hot shooting stretches throughout their careers. Would anybody be surprised if Lundblade came out 3-3 from the arc after being 2 for his last 11 in the last two games? Remember what Hill in the tourney last year? Juke Harris was a 2nd Team All-ACC guy on over 21ppg.

Tennessee dropped twelve spots after that last game and now sit 36th on KP but 90th on Torvik no priors. Their no-priors offense also ranks 218thdue to barely being over 1 PPP against Radford and just above 1 PPP against Tennessee State. Even as someone who was a bit down on Tennessee compared to the market entering the season, I can admit that this is still a pretty cheap price to pay. It’s 2.5 in the market while 4 on KenPom, which is probably the additional point+ tacked onto the projection after only beating Tennessee State by 2-possessions.

Michigan State will likely be the public side, but that doesn’t mean they are the wrong side. If this game is played relatively 'normally' (around a 50th percentile outcome), it's probably a Sparty grind out close win.  When lines first released, I definitely leaned their way. The more I have thought it over, there is some worry about the spot and while it has not cropped up yet, I still concerns if this offense is more susceptible to shooting droughts than they have shown in their first couple games. Coming out of scrimmage season, the question with them was whether there was enough spacing as the Fears/Bonke (or Taylor) tandem looked a tad clunky. When Medlock, Jervis, and Scott are going, they will look like they did against Duke. When they combine to shoot 2-12 from the arc, it will look like it did against UConn.  Both these teams will force the other to beat them from the 3P line, and I trust Tennessee's pure shotmaking at home much more.  

There is plenty of data to back Sparty, but boy if this spot doesn't absolutely stink to the high heavens. I am actually looking at a fun Double Result longshot flyer where Tennessee leads at half behind better shotmaking at home early, but Michigan State wins the game at the end.  One of these teams has Jeremy Fears to get the puppies organized down the stretch, and the other still probably has some structural offensive issues to iron out before we see the best version of them. Agree with the total moving down - this has potential to be pretty rockfighty in the halfcourt, but you will likely have to avoid hot perimeter shooting with the volume that both defenses will funnel the other offense into
